items.title: The News Roundup For October 23, 2026 : 1A : NPR
items.excerpt: This week, President Donald Trump announced that he’s spent $300 million on ads this midterm season, with plans to spend another $100 million before Election Day. The battle between President Trump and the press continues. CNN is threatening legal action against the White House after its journalists were denied access to Air Force One. And on Thursday, the White House Correspondent from The Independent was removed from the aircraft. With the midterms less than two weeks away, Trump is putting the pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to end the war with Russia. And, in global news, demonstrations in France began last month with students across the country protesting deteriorating school conditions, staff shortages and dilapidated buildings. But over several weeks, they’ve tapped into broader anger over living costs, public services, and economic and social discontent. The European Commission estimates the Iran war has cost Europe more than $112 billion through disrupted ?trade and energy markets. An estimated 1.4 million people – more than two thirds of Gaza’s population – are facing food insecurity. We cover the most important stories from around the globe in the on the News Roundup. Find more of our programs online. Listen to 1A sponsor-free by signing up for 1A+ at plus.npr.org/the1a.

items.title: Early Edition: October 23, 2026
items.excerpt: RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR ... Russian President Vladimir Putin yesterday said that future talks on a settlement of the war in Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe. Putin said the peace should be in its “final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time.” Vladimir Soldatkin reports for Reuters. Trump on Wednesday called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine, U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal. The sources said the system was working more normally yesterday shortly after their conversation. Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system’s speeds remained capped. Trump yesterday said Musk had restored Ukraine’s Starlink access but declined to comment when asked about if he had spoken to Musk about the matter. Alexander Ward and Lara Seligman report; Jacob Bogage and Kanishka Singh report for Reuters. ... Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov today told reporters that reports that U.S. citizen Stephen James Hubbard was released in exchange for the recent release of Russian war blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk from custody in Montenegro were false. Dmitry Antonov reports for Reuters. A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel is heading towards New York, ship-tracking data viewed by Reuters showed today. The tanker is the first to be transferred to the United States after Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel. ISRAEL-HAMAS WAR Israeli strikes and gunfire in Gaza yesterday killed at least four people, according to local health officials. In Gaza City, a strike on a car killed at least one person, another strike killed a Palestinian man on a bike in the southern city of Khan Younis, and a strike killed a man near Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza. Gunfire killed a woman near the northern Jabalia refugee camp. The Israeli military said it had struck Hamas militants in Gaza City, Khan Younis, and Nuseirat, but that it was not aware of the reported incident in Jabalia. Nidal al-Mughrabi reports for Reuters. WEST BANK DEVELOPMENTS The Israeli military today said they prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron when they shot and killed two men. The IDF said the two men were carrying guns. The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later instructed security forces to cordon off Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank. Shlomo Mor and Sam Mednick report for AP News. ... A pair of studies published today in the Nature Health journal say severe heat killed more than 50,000 people in European cities and towns this summer. Researchers said that the figure is three times as many people as would have died had manmade global warming not occurred. The studies are based on a combination of factors that influence heat-related health risks in particular locations, and the estimates are not based on official death reports. Raymond Zhang reports for the New York Times. The International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Ecosystems yesterday announced that almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs have now been classified as critically endangered. It was the group’s first global assessment of shallow-water reef ecosystems, and it said heat stress because of climate change is the overwhelming reason for the finding. Catrin Einhorn reports for the New York Times. OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS ... Trump yesterday invoked the Defense Production Act and announced that the government would be spending $150 million toward boosting domestic gas and diesel production. The Cold War-era law gives the president broad powers to increase production of resources within the country for national defense purposes. The Energy Department in a press release noted that the incoming cash was “expected to increase U.S. refining output by millions of gallons per day.” Caroline Vakil reports for The Hill.

items.title: US business activity cools in October; strong demand fueling price pressures By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US business activity slowed modestly in October, though robust demand allowed companies to raise prices for goods and services, a sign that inflation could increase further and remain persistently high in the coming months. S&P Global said on Friday its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, slipped to 57.6 this month from a five-year high reading of 58.4 in September. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. Strength in manufacturing was offset by a slight pullback in the vast services sector. The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing following what is expected to have been a strong performance in the July-September quarter. Economists expect the government’s advance gross domestic product report next week to show the economy growing at around a 3.0% annualized rate last quarter, mainly driven by consumer spending and business investment in AI. The economy has so far not shown any signs of buckling under the weight of the oil price shock stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran, with savings, generous tax returns in the spring, tariff refunds, a strong stock market performance and corporate profits providing a cushion. Economists warned that the inflation fallout from the drawn-out Middle East conflict was likely to slow consumer spending this quarter. ... Its gauge of prices for output rose to 59.8, the highest reading since August 2022, from 58.4 in September. Businesses across manufacturing and services sectors raised prices. Delivery performance by suppliers to manufacturers deteriorated further. The survey’s measure of suppliers’ delivery times dropped to a more than four-year low of 38.1 from 40.9 in September. SUPPLY BOTTLENECKS INTENSIFYING ... "Cost pressures remain a key concern," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers." ... Consumer and producer prices increased strongly in September, the government reported this month, raising concerns that inflation was fanning out across the economy. The Federal Reserve in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range.

items.excerpt: US consumer sentiment nears record low as prices weigh on households ## US consumer sentiment nears record low as prices weigh on households By : ** **Dan Burns / Reuters// October 23, 2026// ** ** People shop for groceries in New York City, August 26, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon/File Photo) US consumer sentiment nears record low as prices weigh on households People shop for groceries in New York City, August 26, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon/File Photo) # US consumer sentiment nears record low as prices weigh on households By : ** **Dan Burns / Reuters// October 23, 2026// ** ** ##### Summary: *– Consumer sentiment fell to its second-lowest level on record.* *– One-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7%.* *– Independent voters reported a sharp drop in economic confidence.* US consumer sentiment edged down to near a record low in October as rising prices beca us e of the Middle East conflict soured ho us eholds’ views of the economy on the doorstep of midterm congressional elections centering on affordability issues, a survey showed on Friday. The University of Michigan‘s Surveys of Consumer s said its Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 48.0 this month from a final reading of 48.1 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index at 46.3, which had also been the index’s preliminary reading for October. October’s reading marked the second- low est on record after the all-time low of 44.8 set in May, not long after the Iran war began. “Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumer s. “ Sentiment is now 10% be low a year ago and 15% less than February, j us t prior to the Iran conflict.” The survey results dovetail with political polling data showing voters have a dim view of the economy and President Donald Trump’s and the Republican Party’s stewardship over it. Millions of US voters have already cast early ballots in the fast-approaching November 3 midterm election that will determine control of Congress over the final two years of Trump’s term. Polls show Republicans are likely to lose control of the Ho us e of Representatives and possibly the Senate as Trump’s approval rating in a Reuters/Ipsos poll sits at a record low thanks to the skyrocketing fuel prices unleashed by his decision to attack Iran in late February. University of Michigan data broken down by political party affiliation showed the weaker sentiment was led by survey respondents self-identified as independents, who comprise a critical bloc of swing voters. Their sentiment score dropped to 42.4 — j us t above May’s record– low 40.6 — from 47.7 in September, while scores for Democrats and Republicans improved. The survey showed a significant upswing this year among independents — and also notably Republicans — citing high prices as a drag on their personal finances. Since January, the number of independents referencing inflation pressures as hurting their financial situation rose by 27%, while it has shot up by 52% among Republicans. Similar citations among Democrats, meanwhile, are up by 15%. Ho us eholds with no or limited exposure to the stock market — until recently climbing rapidly on enth us iasm for the artificial intelligence investment boom — also have cited high prices as a drag on their finances more frequently than at the start of the year. #### Sticky inflation expectations The survey’s measure of consumer expectations for inflation over the next year nudged up to 4.7% from 4.6% in September. Twelve-month inflation expectations have surged from 3.4% in February, before the US-Israeli war with Iran started. Consumer s’ expectations for inflation over the next five years rose to 3.5% from 3.4% in September and 3.2% in March, j us t after the war’s start. Hsu, in an accompanying report on inflation expectations released with the October sentiment survey, said the persistence of elevated inflation expectations in the post-COVID-19 pandemic era posed a risk for Federal Reserve policymakers’ efforts to return inflation to their 2% target — unachieved now for more than five years. “ Consumer s broadly expect inflation to accelerate, and this year’s increases in inflation expectations are not limited to one part of the political spectrum,” Hsu wrote. “The fact that aggregate consumer spending has been relatively resilient despite negative views of the economy provides another reason for caution. If part of consumption currently reflects precautionary spending to avoid future price hikes, disinflation may be even more difficult to achieve.” Fed officials meet next week in Washington, and despite recent higher-than-expected inflation readings in the last two weeks they are broadly expected to leave their policy interest rate unchanged at 3.75%-4.00% after raising it by a quarter percentage point in September. Most Fed officials have indicated they see a need for higher rates, but key leaders also have expressed a willingness to wait for more data before their next move. ## Guthrie-Edmond Regional Airport opens $7M terminal expansion

With the midterms less than two weeks away, Trump is putting the pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to end the war with Russia. And, in global news, demonstrations in France began last month with students across the country protesting deteriorating school conditions, staff shortages and dilapidated buildings. But over several weeks, they’ve tapped into broader anger over living costs, public services, and economic and social discontent. items.title: AP Entertainment SummaryBrief at 6:08 a.m. EDT | Entertainment | wvnews.com
items.excerpt: Why big music stars like Harry Styles and Celine Dion are embracing residencies NEW YORK (AP) — Harry Styles' residency at Madison Square Garden has drawn tens of thousands of fans eager for an exclusive experience. His run is the latest in a trend. Residencies are growing among pop stars, with artists like Bad Bunny, Usher and Carín León embracing the style of performance. Residency pioneer Celine Dion has also returned to the format. Industry insiders say residencies offer benefits like reduced travel stress and elaborate stage productions. However, some fans argue that costs are shifted to them, with high ticket prices and travel expenses to see the shows. While residencies provide artists a break from touring, experts emphasize the importance of traditional tours to reach fans who can't travel. NEW YORK (AP) — An Emmy-winning actor known for roles in “Top Gun” and “Picket Fences,” Tom Skerritt has died at 93. His family said in a statement he died Wednesday of natural causes. Skerritt won an Emmy for “Picket Fences” in 1993 and was known for roles in “Turning Point,” “Steel Magnolias,” and “Contact.” He was once described as a character actor in a leading man’s body. Skerritt also performed onstage, including in “Our Town” and “A Time to Kill.” His family highlighted his passion for storytelling and helping others. ... The beloved children's musician Raffi continues to charm audiences with his timeless songs. Fifty years after his debut children's album, his music remains a staple for young children. Raffi's latest album, “Love is Everywhere,” comes out Friday. It features songs celebrating everything from individuality to the importance of voting. He believes that while technology changes, the essence of childhood remains the same. In an interview with The Associated Press, Raffi emphasized the importance of protecting children's development from excessive technology. He also discussed his commitment to not exploiting children through advertising and how it caused him to turn down a movie offer for “Baby Beluga.” NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Country Music Hall of Famer John Anderson has died at age 71. His family announced his death Wednesday on his social media accounts. Anderson was known for his high, yearning vocal style and hits such as “Swingin’,” “Wild and Blue,” and “Black Sheep.” Born in Apopka, Florida, he moved to Nashville, Tennessee, after high school. He worked odd jobs before his commercial breakthrough in 1977. Anderson was a “New Traditionalist,” sometimes compared to George Jones and Merle Haggard. He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024 and won two Country Music Association awards. LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jay-Z once called John Legend “our voice,” but Pharrell Williams had a different idea for Legend's baritone. On his new album, “Muse,” Legend dials back his powerhouse vocals, opting for a more conversational delivery at Williams’ urging. The album, out Friday, marks Legend’s first full collaboration with Williams after more than 20 years of friendship. Recorded mostly at Williams’ studio in Paris, it grew from Legend’s appearance on Clipse’s “The Birds Don’t Sing.” In an interview, Legend discussed Williams’ influence, Jay-Z’s compliment and composing his first original stage score for a new musical. ... NEW YORK (AP) — Storytelling economy can be in short supply at the movies. But Paweł Pawlikowski has made a career out of a concision that now seems almost radical. His last three films — “Ida,” “Cold War” and his latest, “Fatherland” — are all 90 minutes or less. Each is shot in black and white, in a boxy academy ratio. And none has a single ounce of fat on it. In an era where three-hour movies are commonplace, the 69-year-old Polish filmmaker has refined a style of less is more. His movies are brief but unhurried, lean yet profound. “Fatherland,” starring Sandra Hüller, opens in select theaters Friday.
